transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I... I guess the main thing is I just mostly don't feel like myself anymore. It’s hard to explain, but it’s like the battery is just completely drained out of me, you know? I used to be so active. I mean, I’d be out hiking the trails every single weekend, rain or shine, didn't matter. I was even coaching a youth league, which I loved, I really did, and I’d come home and just strum my guitar to unwind. I had this old acoustic I bought years ago right after I got my degree, and I used to play it every night. But lately... well, for a while now, I just stopped. All of it. I stopped hiking, I quit the coaching, I haven't even taken the guitar out of its case in God knows how long. 

And it's not just the hobbies, it's people too. My phone will ring and I just stare at it. I stopped calling people back entirely. The guys from work, my old friends, they leave voicemails and I just... I can't. Now I just sit in my place. It's this small rental I’ve got, and some days, a lot of days actually, I just sit there in the living room for hours. Just sitting. And the crazy thing is, my brain is telling me the whole time, 'Hey, you need to do laundry, you need to get groceries, you need to pay that bill.' I know there are things to do. I know it. But I just sit there. I physically cannot make myself start doing any of it. It’s just this heavy, empty feeling where I can't get up and just make myself start...
How long have you been feeling this way?

How long? Well... let me really think about that, because it wasn't just an overnight thing, you know? It's not like you wake up one Tuesday and the battery is just gone. But if I really trace it back, look at the timeline of when things started to actually unravel, it was right around the time I moved into this smaller rental I was telling you about. 

That was... gosh, about a year and two months ago, I'd say. Fourteen months. Yeah, because that was right after my divorce was finally finalized. You know how those things go, the lawyers, the paperwork dragging on forever and ever, and then suddenly the judge signs it and you're just... packing up your entire life into cardboard boxes. I had to downsize, obviously, going from the big house we shared to this little place, and I remember telling myself that it was going to be a fresh start. A new chapter, just me and my guitar and the hiking trails. 

But instead of a fresh start, it was like... I don't know, like a string just started pulling on a sweater. First it was just feeling a little tired after hauling all those boxes by myself, but then the weeks went by, and the months went by, and that heavy, empty feeling just settled into my bones. So yeah, about a year and two months of this... this unraveling. Just watching everything slip away while I sit there on the couch staring at the wall, thinking about how it used to be before the move, before the divorce, before everything just completely stopped...
Do you still find pleasure in the things you used to enjoy, or has that changed for you as well?

Pleasure? Gosh, doctor, that's... that's a really big word, isn't it? Pleasure. It's funny you ask it exactly like that, because I was actually just thinking about this the other day when I was looking at that old acoustic guitar sitting in the corner of the room. I mean, I told you I haven't played it in I don't know how long, but it's not just the playing part that's gone. It's the feeling. 

I remember how it used to feel. I used to get this... this warmth in my chest, you know? Like a real, physical sensation of joy when my fingers hit the strings and I got a chord progression just right. Or when I was out on the trails, the smell of the pine trees and the damp earth, it used to make me feel so alive. I'd reach the top of the ridge and just breathe it in, and I felt good. Really, genuinely good. 

But now? Now it's like someone threw a heavy wool blanket over everything. If I try to think about doing those things... if I try to imagine picking up the guitar or lacing up my hiking boots, there's just nothing there. It's completely flat. It's not even that I feel sad about doing them, it's just a void. A blank space where the good feelings used to live. 

Even food, you know? I used to love cooking. I'd make these elaborate Sunday dinners, slow-roasting things for hours, trying out new spices. Now, I eat a piece of toast and it tastes like cardboard. Everything is just cardboard. The music, the hiking, the food... it's all just lost its flavor. I don't know if that makes sense, but it's like the part of my brain that registers anything as enjoyable just completely shut down and locked the door behind it. So no, I don't... I don't find pleasure in any of it anymore. It's all just gone.
Have you had any thoughts about harming yourself or wishing you were dead?

Harming myself? Oh, no. No, doctor, I haven't... I haven't had any thoughts like that. I mean, I know why you're asking, I really do. When you hear someone talking about how everything is just completely flat and how they sit in a chair for hours on end staring at a wall, it makes total sense that you'd wonder if they want to... you know, end it all. It's a logical question. I get it. 

But for me, it's not like that. It's not this intense, burning agony where I want to escape, or where I'm sitting there plotting out some way to hurt myself. It's really just the opposite of intense. It's just... nothing. I don't have the energy to even think about doing something like that, to be perfectly honest with you. The idea of making a plan, or taking some kind of action... it just feels like way too much effort. Everything feels like too much effort, like I was saying before with the laundry and the groceries. 

And as for wishing I was dead... I don't know if I'd call it that, exactly. I don't actively wish for death. I don't go to sleep hoping I won't wake up. It's more just a feeling of existing without really being alive, if that makes any sense at all. Like I'm just taking up space in that little rental house, just breathing in and breathing out, but there's no real point to it. I'm just sort of running out the clock on the day, every single day. But no, I've never once thought about actually hurting myself or trying to speed up the clock, so to speak. That's never crossed my mind. It's just this heavy, endless waiting for nothing in particular.
Do you experience any feelings of worry or fear that are overwhelming or difficult to control?

Worry or fear? Overwhelming worry... let me think about that. You know, it's interesting you bring up fear, especially with my background. Being in protective services, you get trained to handle fear. You get trained to compartmentalize it, to assess a situation, look at the variables, and act. You don't let it overwhelm you, because if it overwhelms you, people get hurt. That was my whole career for over twenty years. I was the guy who kept a cool head when things went sideways. 

But as for right now, sitting here in this state I'm in? No, I wouldn't say I have overwhelming worry or fear. Honestly, doctor, it goes right back to what I was just saying about everything being flat. Fear requires energy. Worry requires you to actually care about the outcome of something. You have to be invested in the future to worry about it, right? You have to think, 'Oh no, what if I lose my job?' or 'What if I can't pay the rent?' or 'What if something bad happens?' 

I don't have that. I don't have the capacity for it right now. If someone told me tomorrow that I was being evicted from that little rental house, I don't even think my heart rate would go up. I'd probably just sit there on the couch and watch them carry the boxes out. It's not bravery, and it's definitely not the kind of controlled, tactical calm I used to have on the job. It's just apathy. It's like the part of my brain that's supposed to sound the alarm bell is just completely disconnected. 

So, no, I don't have these racing thoughts of panic or anxiety. I see people sometimes, you know, at the grocery store—when I actually manage to go—and they look so stressed about the price of eggs or someone cutting in line, and I just look at them like they're from another planet. I can't even fathom having the energy to get worked up over something like that. Or over anything, really. The fear just isn't there. It's just that same heavy, blank nothingness taking up all the space where normal emotions, even the bad ones like fear, are supposed to be.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight recently?

Weight changes... you know, that's a really good question, doctor, but it's one I'm not entirely sure how to answer accurately. Let me try to explain why. Back when I was working, when I was active in the protective services, my weight was something I monitored constantly. It was part of the job requirements, part of the culture, really. You had to stay fit, you had to be ready to move, to run, to handle whatever physical altercation might pop up. I was always around 185 pounds, solid muscle, hitting the gym four days a week, tracking my macros... the whole nine yards. I knew exactly what I weighed on any given Tuesday, you know?

But now? Since everything just sort of... stopped? I honestly haven't stepped on a scale in months. I don't even know where my scale is in that rental house, to be perfectly frank. It might be in the back of the bathroom closet, or maybe it got boxed up and I never unpacked it. I just don't have the motivation to look for it, let alone use it. 

And as for noticing changes just by how my clothes fit or how I look in the mirror... that's tricky too. Like I mentioned before about the food tasting like cardboard, my eating habits are completely shot. Some days I might just eat that one piece of toast because the thought of preparing a meal is just exhausting. Other days, I might mindlessly eat a whole sleeve of crackers while I'm sitting there staring at the wall, not because I'm hungry, but just because they're sitting on the counter. It's totally erratic. 

And my clothes... well, I'm mostly just wearing sweatpants and old t-shirts these days. The same ones, really, since the laundry is such a chore. Sweatpants are pretty forgiving, you know? They have that elastic waistband, so they don't really tell you if you've lost five pounds or gained ten. I haven't put on my old uniform or even a pair of jeans in I don't know how long. If I tried to put on my old tactical pants, maybe I'd notice a difference, but I just don't have any reason to wear them. 

So, I guess the long and short of it is, I don't know. I haven't noticed any significant changes because I haven't been paying attention. I could have lost weight from not eating real meals, or I could have gained weight from just sitting on the couch all day and not moving a muscle. It's just another one of those things that used to be so important, something I tracked so carefully, that has just completely fallen off my radar. It just doesn't seem to matter anymore.
Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?

Moving or speaking more slowly... huh. I mean, I don't think so? It's kind of a hard distinction to make, doctor, given everything else we've just been talking about. 

See, back on the job, everything was about reaction time. You had to be sharp, you had to move fast, speak clearly, give orders, relay information on the radio... it was all very crisp, very deliberate. You couldn't afford to be sluggish. Your brain and your body had to be perfectly in sync, and you were always operating at this high baseline of readiness. 

Now... well, it's not that I feel like I'm moving through molasses, or like I'm speaking in slow motion. It's more about the initiation of the movement, if that makes sense. Like I was saying about the laundry or the groceries, it's the getting up that's the problem. It's the deciding to move. Once I'm actually up, once I finally decide after three hours of staring at the edge of the coffee table that I need to go to the kitchen for a glass of water, I think I just walk to the kitchen at a normal speed. I don't feel heavy or physically slow when I'm actually in motion. I just... don't go into motion very often. I spend most of my time just sitting. 

And with speaking... well, who is there to talk to? I live alone in that rental house. The mail carrier comes by, but I don't go out to say hello. The only time I really use my voice is when I'm here talking to you, or maybe if I have to answer a phone call, which I usually just let go to voicemail anyway because it's just too much effort to engage in a conversation. 

But when I do talk, like right now, I feel like my pacing is normal. I don't feel like my tongue is thick or like my brain is lagging behind my mouth. I think I sound exactly the same as I did five years ago. It's just the desire to speak, the motivation to actually form words and project them into the room... that's what's missing. Not the speed of it. Just the frequency. I could go days without saying a single word out loud, just existing in total silence, and it wouldn't bother me in the slightest. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm moving or talking slower. I'm just... doing a whole lot less of both.
Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure from activities that you used to enjoy, or is it more that you just don't feel like doing them?

Pleasure or just not wanting to... that's the million-dollar question, isn't it? I think... well, mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore. It's like the person I was, the guy who wore the uniform and had a life, he just packed up and left, and I'm just the shell that got left behind. Because it's not just one thing, doctor, it's everything. I used to be so active. I was always doing something. I used to go hiking all the time—up in the state park, you know? I'd load up a pack with forty pounds of gear just to keep my endurance up for the job, and I'd be out there on the trails for six, seven hours at a time, rain or shine. It felt good. I felt alive doing it. 

And I was coaching, too. I used to coach, working with the younger guys, being a leader... I loved that feeling of helping someone else figure things out, building a team, teaching discipline. And when I wanted to unwind after a long shift, I had this old acoustic guitar. I wasn't Eric Clapton or anything, but I could play. I could pick out a tune and just lose myself in the music on a Sunday afternoon. 

But now? I stopped all of it. I stopped hiking, I stopped coaching, I haven't picked up that guitar in... God, I don't even know how long. It's probably covered in an inch of dust right now in the corner of the bedroom. And it's not just the hobbies, it's the people, too. I stopped calling people back. Guys I worked with for a decade will leave a voicemail, "Hey man, just checking in, let's grab a coffee," and I just look at the phone. I look at the screen lighting up, and I know exactly what I should do. I should pick it up, hit dial, and say hello. But I just can't. 

So to answer your question about whether it's the pleasure or the drive... I think the drive is just completely dead. Because some days, I just sit in that small rental for hours. Literally hours, doctor. Just sitting on the couch, staring at the edge of the rug or the blank TV. And the whole time, my brain is ticking away, telling me, "You need to take out the trash. You need to wash a dish. You need to open a window." I know there are things to do. I am fully aware of the list of basic human tasks waiting for me. But I can't make myself start. It's like the starter motor in my chest is completely burned out. I turn the key, and there's just nothing. No spark. No engine turning over. Just sitting there, knowing I should move, and being completely physically and mentally unable to just stand up and do it. So I don't even know if I'd enjoy the guitar or the hiking anymore, because the mountain I have to climb just to get off the couch is already too high.
Do you typically wake up in the morning feeling worse than you do the rest of the day?

Waking up feeling worse... I mean, to be honest with you, doctor, time doesn't really work like that for me anymore. 

Back when I was on the job, mornings were distinct, right? The alarm would go off at 0430, and you're up. You're making the coffee, you're getting a quick workout in, you're lacing up the boots, you've got a briefing at 0600 sharp. There was a rhythm to it all. You knew it was morning because you could feel the energy of the day starting up, you know? You had a purpose the second your feet hit the floor. 

But now... in that rental house... morning is just when the light shifts. It just gets a little brighter coming through the blinds in the living room. That's the only real difference. I don't wake up feeling heavier or worse, and I don't feel any lighter by the evening. It’s just... flat. It’s all exactly the same. I might open my eyes at 7 AM, or maybe it's 11 AM, I don't even bother looking at the clock most days. I just lie there for a while, staring at the ceiling fan—it has this one blade that's slightly warped, I notice it every single time I look up—and I feel exactly the same in that moment as I do at 3 PM when I'm sitting on the couch, or at 9 PM when it gets dark outside again. 

There’s no... there's no fluctuation to it. It's not like there's this dark cloud that's heavier in the morning and then somehow burns off by the afternoon. It’s just a constant, steady state of just... being there. Not really doing anything, just existing in the space. The lack of drive we were just talking about, it doesn't punch a time clock. It's there when I wake up, and it's there when I go to sleep. 

So, if you're asking if the mornings are particularly bad, I'd have to say no. They aren't worse than the afternoons, and the afternoons aren't better than the nights. It all just kind of blurs together into one long, gray stretch of time where nothing really happens. A Tuesday morning feels exactly the same as a Thursday night. So, no, I haven't noticed any difference at all.
Do you feel like your thoughts are slower than they used to be?

Slower thoughts... no, I wouldn't say that. I really wouldn't. It's funny you ask that, actually, because it ties right back into what I was saying about the couch and the lack of drive. My brain isn't moving in slow motion at all. If anything, it's... well, it's not fast, but it's completely normal speed. 

See, when I'm sitting there for three hours staring at the edge of the coffee table, my mind isn't blank, and it's not lagging. I'm sitting there thinking, "Okay, you need to get up. You need to take the trash out. The bags are full, they're going to smell." I'm going through the exact sequence of events in my head at the exact same speed I always would have. I'm planning it all out perfectly. 

Back when I was working, you know, pulling up to a scene, your brain has to process a dozen things in a split second. Who's there, where are the exits, what's the immediate risk... you're evaluating constantly. You can't have a slow brain and do that job. And honestly, my brain still works like that. It still processes information just fine. If I happen to look out the front window of the rental house and see a car parked weird on the street, or someone walking by who doesn't quite fit the neighborhood, I notice it instantly. I process it instantly. The gears up there are turning at the exact same RPM they always did. 

The problem is... it's like the transmission is blown. You know? The engine is revving, the thoughts are happening, the instructions are being sent out from my brain—"stand up, walk to the kitchen, get the water"—but the connection to the wheels is just completely severed. So I'm sitting there, thinking at a perfectly normal pace, fully aware of the time passing, fully aware of every single thing I should be doing, but the physical part just won't engage. 

So, no, the thoughts aren't slow. They're just... trapped in there, I guess. I can think about doing a task a hundred times over in the span of ten minutes, going over every little detail of how I'm going to do it. The speed of the thought is absolutely there. It's just that nothing comes of it.
Do you feel like you're at your worst in the morning?

Wait, didn't we... I feel like we just touched on this a minute ago, didn't we, doctor? About the mornings? Because, like I was saying, I really don't have a "worst" time of day anymore. Or a "best" time, for that matter. It's all just... it's a flatline. 

I know people usually have a rhythm, you know? Like they wake up groggy and feel terrible until they've had their coffee and taken a hot shower, or they hit a wall at 3 PM and feel exhausted. Back when I was in uniform, you definitely had those moments—like that 3 AM slump on a night shift where your eyes feel like sandpaper and you're just praying for the sun to come up. That was a distinct feeling. You knew exactly where you were in the day based on how terrible your body felt.

But now? Now I don't have peaks and valleys. I don't have a "worst." If I'm sitting there at 8 AM, just watching the dust float in the sunlight coming through the gap in those living room blinds, it feels exactly as heavy... exactly as stuck... as it does at 8 PM when the streetlights kick on and shine through that exact same gap. There's absolutely no fluctuation to it. I'm not worse when I wake up, I'm not better by lunch, and I don't crash at night. I'm just exactly where I was. 

It's sort of like being on a treadmill that's unplugged. You're standing on it in the morning, you're standing on it at night, but the belt isn't moving, you haven't gone anywhere, and the scenery hasn't changed an inch. You're just... there. So, yeah, like I mentioned before, the mornings really aren't any worse than the rest of it. It's all just exactly the same.
Have you had any periods in the last year where you felt like your old self again, even if it was just for a little while?

My old self... no. No, doctor, I haven't. Not for a day, not for an hour. It's... well, to really explain it, you have to look at the timeline of everything. 

It hasn't just been a bad week or a rough month. Things have been unraveling since I moved into the smaller rental house. That was right after my divorce was finalized, which... well, that's a whole other story, but the timing is important. That was about a year and two months ago. Fourteen months of just... this. 

I remember packing up the last of my boxes from the house—the house we shared, you know, the one with the nice yard and the garage where I kept all my gear organized perfectly. I moved into this rental, and I remember looking at the boxes stacked in the living room of this new, smaller place. I thought, "Okay, fresh start. You're going to unpack these tomorrow, you're going to set up the coffee maker, you're going to get back on shift, and you're going to push through." 

But tomorrow came, and I didn't unpack the boxes. And then a week went by, and they were still there. And then a month. And now, a year and two months later, some of those boxes are still sitting in the exact same spot in the corner of the living room, gathering dust. I haven't had a single day where I felt like the guy who used to lace up his boots and hit the streets with purpose. That guy hasn't made an appearance since the day I handed over the keys to my old house. 

So, no, there haven't been any periods where I felt like my old self. It's been a steady, continuous unraveling for the last fourteen months, ever since I moved into that rental. It's just been one long, uninterrupted stretch of being stuck right here in this... whatever this is.
Do you feel like you're worse in the morning and it takes you a while to get going?

Doc, are you... did you lose your place in your notes? Because I'm almost positive we just talked about the mornings. Like, literally five minutes ago. 

I know I said my brain isn't slow, but I'm starting to wonder if we're on the same page here, because I really can't emphasize this enough: there is no "worse" in the morning. And as for taking a while to get going... I don't get going. That's the whole point. It's not like I wake up, feel a little groggy, drag my feet for an hour, and then finally get in the shower and start my day. There is no starting the day. 

When I open my eyes... usually around 6 AM, just out of habit from the old shift schedule, my internal clock is still somewhat wired for it... I just look at the ceiling. I can see the texture on the drywall, the little bumps and ridges. I'll just trace them with my eyes. And I know it's morning because the light changes in the room, but my body doesn't feel any heavier or lighter than it did at midnight. I don't need "a while" to get going because the engine never turns over. I could lay there for ten minutes, or I could lay there for four hours, and the feeling is exactly, precisely the same. 

Back in the day, sure, if I pulled a double shift, mornings were rough. You'd hit the snooze button, you'd stumble into the kitchen, you'd wait for that first hit of black coffee to kick in before you even tried to speak to anyone or lace up your boots. That's what taking a while to get going means. You're slow, but you're moving toward something. But this? This isn't a slow start. This is a no start. It's just a continuation of the exact same nothingness from the day before. 

So, no. Like I was trying to explain earlier, the mornings aren't worse. I don't slowly ramp up to feeling okay. I just wake up, and I'm already at the exact same flatline I was at when I went to sleep.
Do you feel like you're more likely to experience a temporary improvement in your mood in response to positive events?

Positive events... I... I don't even know what that would look like right now, to be honest with you. A positive event. What does that even mean anymore? 

I mean, back before all this, sure. If my sergeant commended me on a tough call, or if I finally got that weekend off that I'd been requesting for months, you'd feel that lift, right? You'd feel that rush of, "Hey, things are going my way." You'd grab a beer with the guys after shift, you'd laugh, you'd feel... lighter. Your chest wouldn't feel so tight. 

But now? Let's say... I don't know, let's say my brother calls. He tries, you know, he really does. He'll call and say he got a promotion at his logistics company, or that his kid—my nephew, Tommy—scored the winning goal at his soccer game. And intellectually, in my brain, I know that's a positive event. I know that's a good thing. I know I should feel happy for him, or proud of Tommy. I can remember what it felt like to be proud. 

But when he tells me... it's just words. It's just noise coming through the phone speaker. It doesn't penetrate. It doesn't change the temperature in the room, it doesn't change the weight in my chest. I'll say, "That's great, man, really great," but I'm just reading from a script. Inside, the needle doesn't move a millimeter. It doesn't bump up, not even for a second, not even temporarily. 

It's like... imagine you're wearing a heavy lead vest, like the kind they put on you at the dentist when they take X-rays. And someone comes up and hands you a balloon. They say, "Here, this is a happy balloon, it's a positive thing!" But you're still wearing the lead vest. The balloon doesn't make the vest any lighter. You're still crushed under the exact same weight. 

So, no. If something good happens, if a "positive event" occurs... I don't get a temporary improvement. I don't get any improvement. It just bounces right off the lead vest, and I'm left sitting there, exactly as flat and empty as I was before the phone rang.
Have you experienced a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or lost interest in activities most of the day?

Two weeks? Doc, try the whole fourteen months. Like I keep saying, it's been this one long, continuous stretch since the divorce and moving into that rental. You ask if I lost interest... I mean, mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore. At all. The guy I used to be, he actually had a life. He did things. 

I used to go hiking all the time up at the state park. I had all the gear—the good boots, the hydration packs, the trail maps. Most of that is still taped up in those boxes in the living room I was telling you about. I used to coach, too. Youth baseball. I loved being out there on the diamond, teaching the kids how to field a grounder, just feeling the sun on my neck and being part of the community. I haven't been to a single game or practice since I moved. I didn't even call the league to tell them I was quitting, I just... stopped showing up. 

And my guitar. I have this really nice acoustic guitar, and I used to pick it up almost every evening just to unwind after a rough shift. Now? It's sitting in its case in the corner of the bedroom, gathering dust right alongside everything else. I don't even call people back anymore. My brother, the guys from the old squad, my neighbors... my phone will ring, and I'll just watch the screen light up, watch the caller ID flash, and then watch it go dark. I just can't bring myself to answer or dial them back. 

It's not just that I'm sad, or "depressed" like people say when they have a bad week. It's like I was saying about the mornings—the starter motor is completely shot. Some days, I just sit in that small rental... literally just sit on the edge of the couch or at the kitchen table, for hours. Just sitting there. And the frustrating part is, I'm not brain-dead. I sit there knowing there are things to do. I'll think, 'You need to take out the trash. You need to pay the electric bill. You need to open just one of those boxes.' I know I should do it. I know it would only take a few minutes. But I can't make myself start. There's this massive, invisible wall between knowing I need to do a task and actually moving my muscles to go do it. So I just sit there, for hours on end, trapped in my own living room while the day just drains away.
Do you feel like you're more likely to feel better when something good happens to you, or does it not really make a difference either way?

Doc, wait... didn't you just ask me this? I feel like we're going in circles here. Like, literally two minutes ago you asked about positive events and if my mood improves, and now we're back to... whether good things make me feel better? 

I'm telling you, again, no. It doesn't make a difference either way. It really, truly doesn't. I don't know if I'm just not explaining it right, or if it's just not clicking for you, but I can try to put it another way if that helps, because I want to make sure you're getting this. 

Let's say... I don't know, let's say I won the lottery tomorrow. Just scratched off a ticket and won a million bucks. Most people, they'd be jumping up and down, right? They'd be calling their family, booking a flight to Hawaii, buying a boat, whatever. They'd feel this massive high. Me? I'd probably just stare at the ticket. I wouldn't feel a rush. I wouldn't feel relief. I'd just look at the numbers, know intellectually that I have money now, and then I'd probably just set it on the kitchen counter next to the unpaid electric bill I mentioned earlier, and go back to sitting on the couch. 

Because the money, the "good thing" happening... it doesn't reach me. It's like I'm completely insulated from the rest of the world. It's like trying to listen to the radio when the antenna is snapped off. The signal is out there, the good news is broadcasting, but the machine just can't pick it up. So whether it's my brother calling with good news, or a winning lottery ticket, or just someone bringing me my favorite meal... it does not make a difference. The baseline doesn't move. It's just flat. Always flat. 

Does that make sense? Because I really don't want to keep repeating myself if we're just going to loop back to the exact same question about whether I feel better. I just don't feel better. Ever.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past year?

Weight? No. No, I haven't. Which, honestly, might surprise you, given everything I just said about how I can't even get off the couch to take out the trash. You'd think a guy in my position would just waste away, right? Just forget to eat and drop twenty pounds. But no, my weight has been pretty much exactly the same. It’s just... static. Like everything else in my life right now.

It still processes information just fine. If I happen to look out the front window of the rental house and see a car parked weird on the street, or someone walking by who doesn't quite fit the neighborhood, I notice it instantly. I process it instantly. The gears up there are turning at the exact same RPM they always did. 

The problem is... it's like the transmission is blown. You know? The engine is revving, the thoughts are happening, the instructions are being sent out from my brain—"stand up, walk to the kitchen, get the water"—but the connection to the wheels is just completely severed. So I'm sitting there, thinking at a perfectly normal pace, fully aware of the time passing, fully aware of every single thing I should be doing, but the physical part just won't engage. 

So, no, the thoughts aren't slow. They're just... trapped in there, I guess. I can think about doing a task a hundred times over in the span of ten minutes, going over every little detail of how I'm going to do it. The speed of the thought is absolutely there. It's just that nothing comes of it.

patient.answer:
Wait, didn't we... I feel like we just touched on this a minute ago, didn't we, doctor? About the mornings? Because, like I was saying, I really don't have a "worst" time of day anymore. Or a "best" time, for that matter. It's all just... it's a flatline. 

I know people usually have a rhythm, you know? Like they wake up groggy and feel terrible until they've had their coffee and taken a hot shower, or they hit a wall at 3 PM and feel exhausted. Back when I was in uniform, you definitely had those moments—like that 3 AM slump on a night shift where your eyes feel like sandpaper and you're just praying for the sun to come up. That was a distinct feeling. You knew exactly where you were in the day based on how terrible your body felt.

But now? Now I don't have peaks and valleys. I don't have a "worst." If I'm sitting there at 8 AM, just watching the dust float in the sunlight coming through the gap in those living room blinds, it feels exactly as heavy... exactly as stuck... as it does at 8 PM when the streetlights kick on and shine through that exact same gap. There's absolutely no fluctuation to it. I'm not worse when I wake up, I'm not better by lunch, and I don't crash at night. I'm just exactly where I was. 

It's sort of like being on a treadmill that's unplugged. You're standing on it in the morning, you're standing on it at night, but the belt isn't moving, you haven't gone anywhere, and the scenery hasn't changed an inch. You're just... there. So, yeah, like I mentioned before, the mornings really aren't any worse than the rest of it. It's all just exactly the same.

doctor.question: Have you had any periods in the last year where you felt like your old self again, even if it was just for a little while?

patient.answer:
My old self... no. No, doctor, I haven't. Not for a day, not for an hour. It's... well, to really explain it, you have to look at the timeline of everything. 

It hasn't just been a bad week or a rough month. Things have been unraveling since I moved into the smaller rental house. That was right after my divorce was finalized, which... well, that's a whole other story, but the timing is important. That was about a year and two months ago. Fourteen months of just... this. 

I remember packing up the last of my boxes from the house—the house we shared, you know, the one with the nice yard and the garage where I kept all my gear organized perfectly. I moved into this rental, and I remember looking at the boxes stacked in the living room of this new, smaller place. I thought, "Okay, fresh start. You're going to unpack these tomorrow, you're going to set up the coffee maker, you're going to get back on shift, and you're going to push through." 

But tomorrow came, and I didn't unpack the boxes. And then a week went by, and they were still there. And then a month. And now, a year and two months later, some of those boxes are still sitting in the exact same spot in the corner of the living room, gathering dust. I haven't had a single day where I felt like the guy who used to lace up his boots and hit the streets with purpose. That guy hasn't made an appearance since the day I handed over the keys to my old house. 

So, no, there haven't been any periods where I felt like my old self. It's been a steady, continuous unraveling for the last fourteen months, ever since I moved into that rental. It's just been one long, uninterrupted stretch of being stuck right here in this... whatever this is.

patient.answer:
Doc, are you... did you lose your place in your notes? Because I'm almost positive we just talked about the mornings. Like, literally five minutes ago. 

I know I said my brain isn't slow, but I'm starting to wonder if we're on the same page here, because I really can't emphasize this enough: there is no "worse" in the morning. And as for taking a while to get going... I don't get going. That's the whole point. It's not like I wake up, feel a little groggy, drag my feet for an hour, and then finally get in the shower and start my day. There is no starting the day. 

When I open my eyes... usually around 6 AM, just out of habit from the old shift schedule, my internal clock is still somewhat wired for it... I just look at the ceiling. I can see the texture on the drywall, the little bumps and ridges. I'll just trace them with my eyes. And I know it's morning because the light changes in the room, but my body doesn't feel any heavier or lighter than it did at midnight. I don't need "a while" to get going because the engine never turns over. I could lay there for ten minutes, or I could lay there for four hours, and the feeling is exactly, precisely the same. 

Back in the day, sure, if I pulled a double shift, mornings were rough. You'd hit the snooze button, you'd stumble into the kitchen, you'd wait for that first hit of black coffee to kick in before you even tried to speak to anyone or lace up your boots. That's what taking a while to get going means. You're slow, but you're moving toward something. But this? This isn't a slow start. This is a no start. It's just a continuation of the exact same nothingness from the day before. 

So, no. Like I was trying to explain earlier, the mornings aren't worse. I don't slowly ramp up to feeling okay. I just wake up, and I'm already at the exact same flatline I was at when I went to sleep.

patient.answer:
Positive events... I... I don't even know what that would look like right now, to be honest with you. A positive event. What does that even mean anymore? 

I mean, back before all this, sure. If my sergeant commended me on a tough call, or if I finally got that weekend off that I'd been requesting for months, you'd feel that lift, right? You'd feel that rush of, "Hey, things are going my way." You'd grab a beer with the guys after shift, you'd laugh, you'd feel... lighter. Your chest wouldn't feel so tight. 

But now? Let's say... I don't know, let's say my brother calls. He tries, you know, he really does. He'll call and say he got a promotion at his logistics company, or that his kid—my nephew, Tommy—scored the winning goal at his soccer game. And intellectually, in my brain, I know that's a positive event. I know that's a good thing. I know I should feel happy for him, or proud of Tommy. I can remember what it felt like to be proud. 

But when he tells me... it's just words. It's just noise coming through the phone speaker. It doesn't penetrate. It doesn't change the temperature in the room, it doesn't change the weight in my chest. I'll say, "That's great, man, really great," but I'm just reading from a script. Inside, the needle doesn't move a millimeter. It doesn't bump up, not even for a second, not even temporarily. 

It's like... imagine you're wearing a heavy lead vest, like the kind they put on you at the dentist when they take X-rays. And someone comes up and hands you a balloon. They say, "Here, this is a happy balloon, it's a positive thing!" But you're still wearing the lead vest. The balloon doesn't make the vest any lighter. You're still crushed under the exact same weight. 

So, no. If something good happens, if a "positive event" occurs... I don't get a temporary improvement. I don't get any improvement. It just bounces right off the lead vest, and I'm left sitting there, exactly as flat and empty as I was before the phone rang.

patient.answer:
Two weeks? Doc, try the whole fourteen months. Like I keep saying, it's been this one long, continuous stretch since the divorce and moving into that rental. You ask if I lost interest... I mean, mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore. At all. The guy I used to be, he actually had a life. He did things. 

I used to go hiking all the time up at the state park. I had all the gear—the good boots, the hydration packs, the trail maps. Most of that is still taped up in those boxes in the living room I was telling you about. I used to coach, too. Youth baseball. I loved being out there on the diamond, teaching the kids how to field a grounder, just feeling the sun on my neck and being part of the community. I haven't been to a single game or practice since I moved. I didn't even call the league to tell them I was quitting, I just... stopped showing up. 

And my guitar. I have this really nice acoustic guitar, and I used to pick it up almost every evening just to unwind after a rough shift. Now? It's sitting in its case in the corner of the bedroom, gathering dust right alongside everything else. I don't even call people back anymore. My brother, the guys from the old squad, my neighbors... my phone will ring, and I'll just watch the screen light up, watch the caller ID flash, and then watch it go dark. I just can't bring myself to answer or dial them back. 

It's not just that I'm sad, or "depressed" like people say when they have a bad week. It's like I was saying about the mornings—the starter motor is completely shot. Some days, I just sit in that small rental... literally just sit on the edge of the couch or at the kitchen table, for hours. Just sitting there. And the frustrating part is, I'm not brain-dead. I sit there knowing there are things to do. I'll think, 'You need to take out the trash. You need to pay the electric bill. You need to open just one of those boxes.' I know I should do it. I know it would only take a few minutes. But I can't make myself start. There's this massive, invisible wall between knowing I need to do a task and actually moving my muscles to go do it. So I just sit there, for hours on end, trapped in my own living room while the day just drains away.

I'm telling you, again, no. It doesn't make a difference either way. It really, truly doesn't. I don't know if I'm just not explaining it right, or if it's just not clicking for you, but I can try to put it another way if that helps, because I want to make sure you're getting this.

Does that make sense? Because I really don't want to keep repeating myself if we're just going to loop back to the exact same question about whether I feel better. I just don't feel better. Ever.

But now... cooking? Forget it. The thought of getting out a pan, chopping something up, turning on the stove, and then having to wash the dishes afterward... it's exhausting just thinking about it. It's that invisible wall again. 

So I just eat whatever requires absolute zero effort. A bowl of cereal at two in the afternoon. Maybe I'll order a pizza and just eat cold slices out of the fridge for three days straight so I don't have to think about food again for the rest of the week. Or I'll just grab a handful of crackers from the pantry. And since I'm not hiking, not coaching, not doing anything but sitting in that rental... I'm not burning anything off, either. So it all just balances out into this... nothingness. My clothes all fit exactly the same. I put on my jeans and I use the exact same hole on my leather belt that I've used for the last three years. So no, no weight loss. I'm just carrying around the exact same amount of physical weight, even if everything else feels a thousand times heavier.

Weight gain? No, doc, I just... I just said that, didn't I? I literally just explained this whole thing about my weight like thirty seconds ago. We just talked about this. I haven't lost weight, and I haven't gained weight. It's exactly the same.

Like I was explaining, it's just this weird, static balance. And since I'm just sitting there in the living room, staring at those taped-up boxes, not moving, not burning calories... it just equals out. Appetite? I mean, I guess that kind of goes hand in hand with what I was just saying about the weight and the food, right? But changes in my appetite... I don't know if I'd call it a change in appetite so much as a change in... caring? 

Like, I don't feel hungry, but I don't feel not hungry, either. It's just another thing that doesn't register anymore. Back when I was working, like I said, I was on top of it. I'd wake up, I'd know exactly what I wanted for breakfast. I'd crave things. I'd think, "Man, a steak sounds really good tonight," or "I could go for some tacos." My stomach would rumble, and my brain would say, "Hey, time to eat, go get something good." There was a drive there. A biological drive, sure, but also just a desire to enjoy a meal. 

Now? That drive is just gone. Completely evaporated. My stomach might physically rumble, I guess, but it's like a car alarm going off three blocks away. I hear it, but I don't care. It doesn't make me want to get up and fix it. I don't crave anything. I don't look forward to eating. Food is just... texture. It's just cardboard that I have to chew and swallow so I don't pass out. 

I remember last week, or maybe it was two weeks ago, time is kind of a blur right now... but I realized it was like 8:00 PM and I hadn't eaten anything all day. Not a single thing. And I wasn't even hungry. I only realized it because my head started pounding. So I went to the kitchen, and I just stood there looking in the pantry for a solid ten minutes. Just staring at cans of soup and boxes of pasta. And nothing looked good. Nothing looked bad, either. It just looked like objects. So I grabbed a handful of those dry crackers I mentioned, ate them standing over the sink, and went back to the couch. 

So yeah, I guess my appetite has changed, if you want to call it that. It's just another thing that's flatlined. It's like my body is just running on fumes and it doesn't even bother asking for fuel anymore because it knows I'm not going to put in the effort to get anything good. It's just all so much work, doc. Even chewing feels like a chore. So I just don't think about it unless I absolutely have to.

Good guy, we rode together for four years before I got moved to a different detail. Anyway, he called to tell me his wife just had a baby girl. Their first kid.
